attribution: A collection of verses traditionally regarded as spoken by the Buddha on various occasions; compiled within the early Buddhist community
author: buddha
period: The verses are generally thought to have been gathered in the last centuries BCE, drawing on older material
summary: A collection of 423 verses in the Pali canon on the mind, ethics and the path to liberation, one of the most read Buddhist texts.
whyRead: It is the most accessible entry into early Buddhist teaching as preserved in Theravada. Its short verses on mind, conduct and freedom have been memorised and recited for centuries.
questions: Why does the mind matter so much for happiness and suffering?
What does it mean to be free?

keyTeachings.title: The mind comes first
keyTeachings.text: The collection opens by placing the mind before all experience: actions done with a corrupted mind lead to suffering, and those done with a clear mind to happiness.

keyTeachings.title: Hatred is not ended by hatred
keyTeachings.text: A famous early verse teaches that enmity is ended by its absence, not by retaliation, a principle often cited in Buddhist ethics.

keyTeachings.title: The three marks
keyTeachings.text: A group of verses states that all conditioned things are impermanent (anicca) and unsatisfactory (dukkha), and that all phenomena are without self (anatta).

keyTeachings.title: The summary of the teaching
keyTeachings.text: A verse often quoted as a summary of the Buddhas' teaching recommends avoiding harm, cultivating the good and purifying the mind.

keyTeachings.title: The awakened person
keyTeachings.text: Later chapters describe the arahant and the true brahmin as one defined by conduct and freedom from craving, not by birth.

structure.label: Place in the canon
structure.note: Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka in the Pali canon

structure.label: Commentary
structure.note: The Pali commentary with stories for each verse is traditionally attributed to Buddhaghosa

structure.label: Parallels
structure.note: Related collections survive in Gandhari, Sanskrit (Udanavarga) and Chinese
